Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR  

* **MapLibre Native on Android cannot skip the `glyphs` field completely** – the engine will abort a style that has no glyphs URL.  
* What you *can* do is **serve the glyph files from the device itself** (e.g. from the app’s `assets/` or `raw/` folder) and **use the `font-faces` property** to point each `text-font` name at a bundled TTF/OTF.  
* With that combination the map draws every label with the **local font files** you ship, and you never need an external HTTP glyph server.  

Below is a step-by-step recipe that works for all scripts (Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, CJK, …) and keeps the app 100 % offline.

---

## 1. Why you still need a `glyphs` URL

| SDK | Behaviour when `glyphs` is missing |
|-----|--------------------------------------|
| **MapLibre GL JS** (≥ 5.11) | Falls back to the TinySDF local-font renderer – you can omit `glyphs` entirely. |
| **MapLibre Native** (Android, iOS) | **No fallback** – the style is considered invalid and the map will not render. The issue is tracked as [#165](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/165). |

Therefore, for an offline Android app you must give the engine *some* URL template, even if the files it points at never contain real glyph data. The engine will ignore those files as soon as a matching entry exists in `font-faces`.

---

## 2. Bundle the fonts you want to use

1. **Pick the font files** (TTF/OTF) you want for each script.  
   *For a “global” map the easiest choice is the Noto family* – it covers Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Devanagari, Thai, CJK, etc.  
2. **Copy them into the Android project** (e.g. `app/src/main/assets/fonts/`).  
   ```
   app/
   └─ src/
      └─ main/
         └─ assets/
            └─ fonts/
               ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf
               ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
               ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
               └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf
   ```
3. (Optional) **Compress the assets** with `aaptOptions { noCompress "ttf","otf" }` in `build.gradle` so Android does not try to zip-compress them at runtime.

---

## 3. Declare the `font-faces` block in your style JSON

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",   // <-- dummy URL, see §4
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"]   // Latin, Latin-Extended
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans CJK SC": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"]
      }
    ]
  },

  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans CJK SC",
          "Noto Sans Arabic",
          "Noto Sans Devanagari",
          "Noto Sans Regular"
        ]
      }
    }
    /* … other layers … */
  ]
}
``*Key points*

* **`text-font` is a *fallback list*** – the first entry that has a matching `unicode-range` in `font-faces` wins.  
* The **`url` must be a scheme the Android runtime can resolve** (`file://` works for assets, `android.resource://` works for `res/raw/` files).  
* **`glyphs` can point anywhere** – we’ll give it a dummy path that resolves to an empty folder (see next section). The engine will never ask for those glyph PBFs because the `font-faces` entries already satisfy every code-point.

---

## 4. Provide a *dummy* glyph-server path (offline)

Create an **empty folder** in `assets/glyphs/` that mirrors the `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` hierarchy, e.g.:

```
assets/
└─ glyphs/
   └─ Noto%20Sans%20Regular/
      └─ 0-255.pbf   (empty file, 0 bytes)
```

You only need **one empty `.pbf`** per font-stack you reference; the engine will request the range that contains the code-point, get a 0-byte response, and then fall back to the `font-faces` file.  

If you prefer not to ship empty files, you can also start a **tiny local HTTP server** (e.g. using `NanoHTTPD`) that always returns `404`. The native SDK treats a missing glyph range the same way – it simply skips the PBF and uses the local font.

---

## 5. Load the style in Android

```kotlin
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibreMap
import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapView

class OfflineMapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)   // initialise the SDK
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_offline_map)

        mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView)
        mapView.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // The style JSON can be a raw asset, a string, or a URL on the device.
        val styleUri = "file:///android_asset/style-offline.json"

        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap: MapLibreMap ->
            mapboxMap.setStyle(
                Style.Builder().fromUri(styleUri)
            ) { style ->

                // If you need to modify font-faces at runtime:
                // style.setFontFaces(fontFacesMap)

                // Optional: enable debug logging to see that glyphs are *not* used
                Log.i("MapLibre", "Style loaded – all labels will use bundled fonts")
            }
        }
    }

    // … lifecycle callbacks (onStart, onStop, …) …
}
```

* `styleUri` points to the JSON you created in §3.  
* The `glyphs` field inside that JSON points to the dummy `file:///android_asset/glyphs/...` path, so the SDK never tries to hit the network.  

---

## 6. What about CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean)?

* **Native does not have the `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut that GL JS uses.**  
* By bundling a CJK font in `font-faces` (as shown above) you get the same effect: the engine draws the ideographs from the local TTF/OTF instead of requesting thousands of glyph ranges.  
* **Do *not* ship the huge Noto CJK PBF set** – it would be many megabytes and is unnecessary when you have the TTF/OTF locally.

---

## 7. Summary checklist

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| 1 | Add the desired TTF/OTF files to `assets/fonts/` (or `res/raw/`). |
| 2 | Write a `font-faces` block that maps each `text-font` name to the local `file://` URL and restricts it with `unicode-range`. |
| 3 | Keep a **dummy `glyphs` URL** (e.g. `file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) and optionally ship one empty `.pbf` per font-stack. |
| 4 | Use the same `text-font` fallback list in your symbol layers. |
| 5 | Load the style with `MapLibre.getInstance(...).setStyle(...)` as shown. |
| 6 | Test on a device with **airplane mode** – all labels should still appear, using the bundled fonts. |

If you later decide you *do* want to serve real glyph PBFs (e.g. for a very small-size font that you cannot ship as a TTF), just replace the dummy `glyphs` URL with a real local HTTP endpoint and keep the `font-faces` entries – the engine will automatically prefer the PBFs when they exist and fall back to the local font otherwise.

---

| No text at all (layer invisible) | `glyphs` URL points to a non-existent folder **and** `font-faces` entry is missing or miss-spelled. | Verify the `text-font` name exactly matches the key in `font-faces`. |

Description: explicit — right-to-left Arabic and Hebrew labels on GL JS 6

## TL;DR | What you need | How to do it | |---------------|--------------| | **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.9.0** (the version you already have) | No extra plugin – the engine now shapes Arabic/Hebrew itself. | | **A font that contains the Arabic/Hebrew glyphs** (e.g. *Noto Sans Arabic* / *Noto Sans Hebrew*) | Add the font name to every layer that draws place-name text (`text-font`). | | **A `glyphs` URL or `font-faces` entry** that points at the same font (or rely on the GL-JS local-font fallback) | Either keep the style’s `glyphs` pointing at a glyph-PBF server **or** omit `glyphs` and let GL JS load the font locally. | | **`text-direction: "right-to-left"`** (optional – GL JS will infer it from the script) | Set it on the layer if you want to force RTL for mixed-script labels. | | **(If you ever run an older GL JS < 6.9.0)** | Load the RTL-text plugin **once**, before creating the map. | Below is a step-by-step guide that covers the *current* way (GL JS ≥ 6.9.0) and also shows the legacy fallback for older versions. --- ## 1. Verify you are really on GL JS ≥ 6.9.0 ```js import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; console.log('MapLibre version →', maplibregl.version); // Must be 6.9.0 or newer for built-in RTL shaping. ``` If you are on 6.8.x or older, upgrade (or use the legacy plugin – see § 5). --- ## 2. Using a **glyph-PBF server** (the classic path) If you already have a `glyphs` URL (e.g. `https://mytileserver.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`), make sure the server contains the Noto Arabic/Hebrew stacks: ``` /Noto%20Sans%20Arabic%20Regular/0-255.pbf /Noto%20Sans%20Arabic%20Regular/256-511.pbf … /Noto%20Sans%20Hebrew%20Regular/0-255.pbf … ``` You can copy the pre-built PBFs from the **openmaptiles/fonts** or **UNDP-Data/fonts** repositories and serve them yourself. ### 2-b. **Local-font fallback** (no glyph server needed) Since GL JS 5.11.0 you can *omit* the `glyphs` property entirely. The engine will then resolve every `text-font` name as a **web or system font**, exactly like CSS `font-family`. This is perfect for offline or self-hosted apps. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": null, // <-- omit or set to null "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` > **Tip:** If you host the fonts on the same origin as your web page, you can use relative URLs (`"./fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf"`). Otherwise make sure CORS headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your domain) are present. --- ## 3. The weight keyword (`"bold"`) in the `text-font` list works the same as in CSS. --- ## 4. Verify that shaping works Arabic and Hebrew are *joining* scripts: letters change shape depending on their neighbours. After the steps above, you should see: * **Arabic** – letters connected, proper initial/medial/final forms, and the whole word rendered right-to-left. * **Hebrew** – right-to-left order, with any diacritics (niqqud) positioned correctly. Ensure the `text-font` name matches exactly the entry in `font-faces` or the glyph-PBF server. | | Text appears **left-to-right** (even though the script is Arabic) | `text-direction` is set to `"left-to-right"` somewhere, or the layer’s `text-font` list does not contain an Arabic/Hebrew font, causing the engine to fall back to a Latin font that forces LTR. | | No text at all (transparent) | The glyph-PBF request failed and you are on a **Native** build (which has no local fallback). Provide a working `glyphs` URL or add `font-faces` entries. | | Mixed-script labels (Arabic + Latin) look odd | Use a **fallback list** that includes both Arabic and a Latin font, e.g. `["Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]`. The engine will switch fonts per-character automatically. | --- ## 5. (Legacy) If you ever have to run GL JS < 6.9.0 Older versions cannot shape Arabic/Hebrew on their own. You must load the **RTL-text plugin** *once*, **before** creating the map: ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; // Load the plugin from a CDN or your own copy. setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/@mapbox/mapbox-gl-rtl-text@0.3.0/dist/mapbox-gl-rtl-text.js', /* lazy */ false // true = load on-demand; false = load immediately ); ``` After the plugin is registered, the rest of the steps (font, `text-font`, etc.) are identical. Full minimal example (GL JS ≥ 6.9.0, local-font fallback) ```html Arabic & Hebrew labels
``` *Replace the `url` values with the real locations of your font files.* The map will now render Arabic and Hebrew place names correctly, with proper joining and right-to-left direction. --- ## 7. Quick checklist | ✅ | Item | |----|------| | **GL JS version** ≥ 6.9.0 (or load RTL plugin for older) | | **`glyphs`** – either a working glyph-PBF URL **or** `null` (local fallback) | | **`font-faces`** entry (if using local fallback) that points at a TTF/OTF containing Arabic/Hebrew | | **`text-font`** list includes the Arabic/Hebrew font name (exact match) | | **`text-direction`** set to `"right-to-left"` *or* left to default auto-detect | | **CORS** – fonts served with proper `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` if cross-origin | | **Test** – verify joined forms appear; if not, check console for “Unable to load glyph …” or “Failed to load font …” errors | Follow these steps and your Arabic and Hebrew place-name labels will render correctly, with proper right-to-left ordering and contextual letter shaping.
